summary: For ages 6–7, children learn that a simple food chain shows food-energy passing along a sequence that always starts with a plant (a producer that makes its own food) and flows to animals (consumers). The crux is the arrow convention: the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to' and points from the food to the feeder. Activities span building and drawing a three-link chain, interpreting a given labelled chain, checking structure through ordering and matching, and talking through an organism's place in the chain including what happens if the producer is lost. Aligns with UK DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'.
misconceptions: Drawing arrows the wrong way (pointing from the eater to the food).
Starting a food chain with an animal instead of a plant.
Thinking the arrow means 'eats' rather than 'energy/food flows to'.
Believing plants get their food by eating, like animals, rather than making it.
Treating the top predator as the 'start' or most important, rather than the producer.

activities.title: Build and arrow a three-link food chain
steps: Arrange organism cards (grass, rabbit, fox) into the correct order, left to right.
Draw an arrow between each pair of organisms, pointing from the one that is eaten to the one that eats it.
Say aloud what each arrow means: 'is eaten by / the food and energy pass to the next animal.'
Label each link as 'producer' (the plant) or 'consumer' (each animal).
Explain why the chain must begin with the plant: the grass makes its own food, but the rabbit and fox must eat to get theirs.
activities.insight: Every food chain starts with a plant that makes its own food, and arrows track food-energy flowing from the eaten to the eater.

activities.title: Interactive chain reference: read the roles and the arrow
steps: Tap or point to each organism to reveal its role: 'I eat… / I am eaten by…' and whether it is a producer or consumer.
Tap or point to each arrow to reveal that it means 'is eaten by / energy flows to'.
Retell the chain in your own words, naming producer and consumer and reading each arrow correctly.
activities.insight: The arrow carries a fixed meaning ('is eaten by / energy flows to') and each organism has a role (producer or consumer) that stays consistent across the chain.

activities.title: Order the chain and choose the starting rule
steps: Put a scrambled set of organisms (grass, rabbit, fox) into the correct chain order.
Answer: 'What does every food chain start with?' and choose the plant/producer.
Answer an arrow-direction item: which way does the arrow point between two organisms?
Match each organism to its label: 'producer' or 'consumer'.
activities.insight: A food chain has a fixed structure — producer first, then consumers — and the arrow direction and role labels can be identified reliably.

activities.title: Talk through an animal's place in the chain
steps: Take the part of one animal in the chain (e.g. the rabbit).
Answer: 'What do I eat?' and 'Who eats me?'
Name what comes before you (your food) and after you (your eater) in the chain.
Trace the whole chain back to the plant that makes its own food.
Consider what would happen to the fox if all the grass died out, and explain how the whole chain depends on the plant at the start.
activities.insight: Each animal sits between what it eats and what eats it; following those links backwards always reaches a plant, and because every animal ultimately depends on the producer, losing the plant affects the whole chain.

checkQuestion: Say: 'A rabbit eats grass, and a fox eats the rabbit. I want you to draw this as a food chain with arrows, and tell me what each arrow means. Then tell me: why must the chain start with the grass and not with the fox?'
checkAnswer: Arrows point grass → rabbit → fox, and an arrow means 'is eaten by' / the food and its energy pass to the next animal. The chain starts with grass because a plant is a producer — it makes its own food using sunlight, so it is the source of food and energy that everything else depends on; animals are consumers and cannot make their own food.
